Never, at any timescale relevant to a house. The premise is a myth.

Glass is an amorphous solid, not a flowing liquid. At room temperature its viscosity is so high that estimates of the time for measurable flow exceed the age of the universe by many orders of magnitude. Medieval cathedral glass would not have visibly sagged in 800 years, and studies of old glass (e.g., Zanotto, 1998) back this up.

Old panes are uneven because of how they were made. Crown glass was spun into a disk, giving variable thickness. Cylinder glass was also irregular. Glaziers often installed panes with the thicker edge down for stability, which created the "thicker at the bottom" look. Some old panes are thicker at the top or sides, which flow couldn't explain.

Modern float glass is uniform and will stay flat for as long as the window exists. Sagging you might see in a house window is from the frame or installation (settling, failed spacers or seals in insulated units), not the glass itself.
